extracted.intended_audience: college faculty, curriculum committees, administrators, and tutors designing or running quantitative literacy/quantitative reasoning programs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for designing, implementing, staffing, assessing, and sustaining college-level quantitative literacy / quantitative reasoning requirements, courses, tutorials, and tutoring centers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods for demonstrating quantitative literacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Students must demonstrate basic quantitative literacy by passing a Quantitative Skills Exam given to all first-year students and transfers during Orientation, by passing a designated quantitative course, or by completing a non-credit tutorial. Requirement should be completed by the end of the first year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advisors meet with first-year students and transfers before fall registration to discuss exam results and plan fulfillment. Offerings that satisfy the requirement typically change year to year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative Skills Exam — pass threshold and diagnostic purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The Quantitative Skills Exam is used both as a gate/requirement (Hamilton example: passing defined as 50%, i.e., 14/28 correct) and as a diagnostic tool to identify students with quantitative deficiencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The exam is largely high-school level multiple-choice; concerns exist about the adequacy of using a 50% multiple-choice cutoff to certify competency. To be useful diagnostically, results should be itemized to inform advisors about specific skill gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment of assessment with instructional content
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment instruments (exams) should be aligned with the material actually taught (e.g., a new exam tailored specifically to non-credit tutorial modules was created to better measure mastery).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When tutorials or courses have narrowly focused modules, exams should be consistent with those modules to better measure student mastery and to provide fair diagnostic information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-credit tutorial design and core modules
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-credit tutorial should be a self-paced, tutor-based, grade-free mini-course available through the Quantitative Literacy Center, intended for students willing to sharpen skills without course credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton’s tutorial consists of four main modules: I. Basic Computation, II. Algebraic Expressions, III. Graphs and Charts, IV. Proportional & Functional Reasoning. Tutorials run about ten weeks; students are encouraged to attend regularly and make up missed sessions. Emphasize relevance and accessibility for 'math-phobic' students and transferability to life-skills (e.g., personal finance, nutrition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tutor selection, training, and supervision
rubrics_metrics.description: Undergraduate tutors are chosen from nominees submitted by faculty and receive training and supervision before and during the year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initial training covers learning styles, tutoring strategies, multicultural settings, and communication. Staff meetings are held throughout the semester; tutors meet at least once per semester with the Quantitative Literacy Committee. Tutors should be competent, well-trained, carefully supervised, and act as mentors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Center operating hours, staffing breadth, and physical resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative Literacy Center functions as a drop-in clinic with specified hours (evenings and some afternoons) and aims to have representation from most disciplines when open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make computer resources available when courses require them. The Center is typically housed adjacent to administrative offices; overflow tutoring can use neighboring classrooms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tracking and documentation of tutoring interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use sign-in logs and require tutors to submit detailed reports of their work that list student names, courses tutored, problems worked on, and an assessment of helpfulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This documentation helps the Director track student progress and respond to inquiries from instructors or advisors about a student's difficulties.

rubrics_metrics.name: User feedback through periodic questionnaires
rubrics_metrics.description: Distribute semester questionnaires to students who used the Center asking how they found out about the Center, frequency of use, tutor helpfulness, willingness to return, and whether they'd recommend it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questionnaire results produce qualitative feedback (e.g., students value convenient hours, home-base feeling, but may be frustrated when tutors don't give answers). Use this feedback for program improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course designation and consistency criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria for labeling a course as satisfying the quantitative literacy requirement must account for variability in course content across instructors and semesters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because course content and quantitative intensity can change with different instructors, the Committee should regularly revisit and update the list of qualifying courses and be cautious about labeling courses whose quantitative content is not uniform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faculty engagement and incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase faculty understanding and commitment to the program through communication, advising improvements, workshops, and incentives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested actions include: inform faculty about the requirement, educate students about their responsibilities, improve advising systems, offer workshops (e.g., using a Writing Across the Curriculum model) on using quantitative literacy in the classroom, and offer stipends to faculty who attend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program assessment and outcome measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Programs should have systematic, comprehensive assessment plans rather than relying primarily on qualitative/anecdotal results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment should include analysis of correlations between placement/exam scores and subsequent course grades, itemized exam reporting to identify skill gaps, tracking of tutorial completion, and measurable outcome indicators rather than only anecdotal feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy on prerequisites vs. remediation sequencing
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarify the institutional policy on whether demonstrated proficiency (exam passage) should be a prerequisite for enrollment in quantitatively demanding courses, or whether students should be required to enroll in such courses to become proficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'chicken-and-egg' policy decision affects advising, student placement, and enforcement; make the policy explicit to ensure follow-through and better alignment of course sequencing with student preparedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative Reasoning (QR) course core content requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Any course designated as a Quantitative Reasoning course must cover descriptive statistics, linear models, and exponential models or probability, and must include use of technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The course should emphasize reasoning and appropriate quantitative analysis rather than rote manipulation; technology (graphing calculators or computers) should be integrated into instruction and activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: QR pedagogy — investigations, collaborative work, and technology
rubrics_metrics.description: QR courses should follow an investigations pedagogy with extensive collaborative learning and technology use, integrating activities such as data analysis, group projects, presentations, and written analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer data-driven examples and real-world problems, hold class meetings in computer labs when possible, require analytic writing and formal presentations, and include in-class and out-of-class projects to build transferable quantitative reasoning skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embedding general education principles in QR courses
rubrics_metrics.description: Five general education principles must be embedded: critical reading and analysis; effective speaking/listening/writing; logical and quantitative reasoning; use of technology to further learning; and independent and collaborative work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additionally, students should generalize and apply QR strategies to topics outside the course and write quantitative arguments clearly and concisely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class size limit to optimize learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Each section of a Quantitative Reasoning course should be limited to fewer than 25 students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small sections help faculty give attention to principles and optimize student mastery, particularly given the collaborative, technology-intensive pedagogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement testing and pathways
rubrics_metrics.description: Use standardized placement tests (e.g., ACCUPLACER for freshmen; department-designed tests for transfers) to place students into developmental math, Quantitative Reasoning, or College Algebra, with exemptions for those demonstrating higher proficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Placement results determine appropriate course pathways; advising should steer students (e.g., intended science/management majors should be advised to take College Algebra or Precalculus rather than QR).

rubrics_metrics.name: Course sequencing and articulation (pathways)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define clear pathways through mathematics courses (e.g., Math Skills -> Quantitative Reasoning -> Statistics/Research Methods; or College Algebra -> Precalculus -> Calculus) to guide advising and progression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make explicit which pathways feed into major requirements and graduate expectations; provide waivers or transfer-credit rules where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: QR courses designed to be non-terminal and preparatory
rubrics_metrics.description: QR courses should not be terminal; they should prepare students to move into other mathematics or discipline-specific quantitative courses and foster deeper understanding of posing and analyzing real-world problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courses should lead naturally into statistics, research methods, or major courses and incorporate examples from a wide variety of disciplines to encourage transferability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on real data and real-world applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce new topics using datasets or real-world motivations so students can apply quantitative reasoning to meaningful contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include analyzing news articles or public data (Boston Globe budget example), comparing linear vs. exponential growth, and weekly activities involving current data sources; this approach helps reduce math anxiety and emphasizes reasoning over abstract manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale-driven content choices (e.g., exponential vs. probability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose content emphases based on pedagogical goals (UMass chose exponential modeling over probability to broaden modeling experience and deepen understanding of growth distinctions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document rationale for content selections so faculty and students understand expected learning outcomes and how topics support modeling and decision-making skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of challenging, multi-step problems for assessment and growth
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess students with multi-step, reading- and writing-intensive problems that may be challenging initially but should show measurable improvement by the final exam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide examples of such problems and expect that repeated practice, writing, and group work will lead to students successfully completing these problems by semester end; use these tasks as summative measures of QR competency.
